la:noun:ingenium.gloss: innate or natural quality, natural character; nature
senses: innate or natural quality, natural character; nature
a person of genius, a genius, a highly skilled or accomplished person
la:noun:ingenium.html:
ingĕnĭum, ii, n.
in-geno, from gigno
,
innate or natural quality, nature.
In gen. (so mostly poet.; in Sall. and in postAug. prose; not in Cic. or Cæs.): pro ingenio ego me liberum esse ratus sum, pro imperio tuo tibi servire aequom censeo,: ite in frundiferos locos Ingenio arbusta ubi nata sunt, non obsita, by their own nature, Naev. ap. (Trag. Rel. v. 28 Rib.); so, loci, Dietsch: locorum hominumque ingenia,; ; ; : terrae,: montis,; cf.: campi suopte ingenio humentes,: arvorum,; and, portūs,: arbores sui cujusque ingenii poma ferunt,: lactis ingenia et proprietates,: ingenium velox igni, Sev. Aetn. 214: crines ingenio suo flexi,naturally,: ut magistratus imperio suo vehemens mansueto permitteretur ingenio,; cf.: cum honesta suopte ingenio peterentur,in consequence of its own nature,: mitis ingenio,: cunctator ingenio,: ingenio trux,.— Rarely of beasts: mitior ad feras bestias, praecipitia ingenia sortitas,.—
In partic., of persons.
Natural disposition, temper, mode of thinking, character, bent, inclination: feci ego ingenium meum,have acted out,: ita ingenium meumst,: ut ingenium est omnium hominum ab labore proclive ad lubidinem,: liberale,: pium ac pudicum,: durum atque inexorabile,: inhumanum,: lene in liberos,: utinam nunc matrescam ingenio, Rib. (1 Rib., maturescam): mobile,: cicur et mansuetum, Müll.: inverecundum animi,: vera loqui etsi meum ingenium non moneret. : ingenio suo vivere,: redire ad ingenium, to return to one's natural bent, to one's old courses, : Volscis levatis metu suum rediit ingenium,: quae maxime ad muliebre ingenium efficaces preces sunt, : vanum dictatoris,: mitis ingenii juvenem,: Turni ferox,: temperare suum,to control his temper,: horrida,: molliora,: humana,: felix,: rapax,: atrox,: procax,: ingenium ingeni, in Plautus, signifies peculiarity of disposition, Stich. 1, 2, 69.—
Concr. collect.: tanto corruptius iter immixtis histrionibus et spadonum gregibus et cetero Neronianae aulae ingenio,the people who gave character to the court,.—
With respect to intelligence.
Natural capacity, talents, parts, abilities, genius: docilitas, memoria, quae fere appellantur uno ingenii nomine,: ingenium ad fingendum,: excellens ac singulare,: vir acerrimo ingenio,: cujus tanta vis ingenii est, ut, etc.,: tardum,: acutum aut retusum,: eximium,: praestantissimum,: magnum,: illustre,: oratorium,: pulcherrimum et maximum,: hebetatum, fractum, contusum,: celeres ingenii motus,: ingenii acies,: ingenii lumen,: ingenii vis,: ingenii vena,: ingenii vigor,: ingenii celeritas,: ingenii docilitas,: ingenio abundare,: ingenio valere,: ingenio divino esse,: ingenio hebeti esse,: in eo ingenium ejus elucere videbatis,: colere et imbuere ingenium artibus,: acuere,: alere,: exercere multiplici variāque materiā,: versabatur in hoc nostro studio cum ingenio,with cleverness,; so, cum ingenio,: ingenii memoria immortalis est,.— Plur.: acutiora ingenia et ad intellegendum aptiora eorum, qui, etc.,: aliae (partes agrorum) quae acuta ingenia gignant, aliae quae retusa,intellects, —
Transf.
A genius, i. e. a man of genius, a clever, ingenious person: excepi voluntatem tam excellens ingenium fuisse in civitate,; ; : nullum magnum ingenium sine mixtura dementiae fuit,. — Plur.: ut saepe summa ingenia in occulto latent,: decora,: magna,: nostra (i. e. oratores,; ; ; : candidissimus omnium magnorum ingeniorum aestimator Livius,: ingenia et artes vel maxime fovit,; : id in magnis animis ingeniisque plerumque contingit,.—
Of things, an invention, a clever thought: exquisita ingenia cenarum,; cf. : noctium suarum ingenia (= flagitiosae libidinis inventiones),voluptuous inventions,.

la:adj:ingenuus.html:
ingĕnŭus, a, um, adj.
ingeno, ingigno
.
Native, indigenous, not foreign.
Lit.: fontes,: tophus,produced in the country,.—
Transf., inborn, innate, natural: inest in hoc amussitata sua sibi ingenua indoles,: color,natural color,. —
Free-born, born of free parents.
In gen.: ingenuus homo meant formerly one born of a certain or known father, who can cite his father: en unquam fando audistis patricios primo esse factos, non de caelo demissos, sed qui patrem ciere possent, id est nihil ultra quam ingenuos,: ingenui clarique parentes,; .—Esp., subst.: ingĕnŭus, i, m., and ingĕnŭa, ae, f., a free-born man or woman: ingenui sunt qui liberi nati sunt; libertini, qui ex justa servitute manumissi sunt,: tutela liberantur ingenuae, etc.,; but this word differs from liber, inasmuch as the latter signifies also a freedman,: ingenuamne an libertinam,: omnis ingenuorum adest multitudo,: Patricios Cincius ait appellari solitos, qui nunc ingenui vocentur, Paul. ex Müll.: libertinos ab ingenuis adoptari posse, Masur. ap. .—
In partic.
Worthy of a freeman, noble, upright, frank, candid, ingenuous (syn. liberalis): nihil apparet in eo ingenuum,; : timiditas,: dolor,: vita,: est animi ingenui (with inf.), : ingenuis studiis atque artibus delectari,: (with humanae) artes,: ingenui vultus puer ingenuique pudoris,: amor,: per gemitus nostros ingenuasque cruces,and by such sufferings on the part of a freeman as belong only to slaves,: fastidium,: aperte odisse magis ingenui est, quam, etc.,: astuta ingenuum vulpes imitata leonem,.—
Weakly, delicate, tender (free-born persons being less inured to hardships than slaves; poet.): invalidae vires, ingenuaeque mihi,: gula,.—Hence, adv.: ingĕnŭē, in a manner befitting a person of free or noble birth, liberally; openly, frankly, ingenuously: educatus,: aperte atque ingenue confiteri,; : pro suis dicere,.

la:adj:ingeniosus.gloss: superior in intellect, gifted with genius; intellectual, clever, ingenious
senses: superior in intellect, gifted with genius; intellectual, clever, ingenious
la:adj:ingeniosus.html:
ingĕnĭōsus (ingĕnŭ-), a, um, adj.
ingenium
,
intellectual, superior in intellect, endowed with a good capacity, gifted with genius, of good natural talents or abilities, clever, ingenious.
Lit.: Aristoteles quidem ait, omnes ingeniosos melancholicos esse,: ingeniosi vocantur,: vir ingeniosus et eruditus,: quo quisque est solertior et ingeniosior,: homo ingeniosissimus,: ad aliquid,: dandis ingeniosa notis,: esse in aliqua re, Mart. praef. 1: in poenas,: res est ingeniosa dare,giving requires good sense,. —
Transf., of inanimate things.
Ingenious, clever: argumentum,.—
Adapted to, apt, fit for any thing: vox mutandis ingeniosa sonis,: terra ingeniosa colenti,: ad segetes ager,.—Sup.: ingenuosissimus,.— Adv.: ingĕnĭōsē, acutely, wittily, ingeniously: tractantur ista ingeniose,: electas res collocare,: dicere,.— Comp., .— Sup.: homo ingeniosissime nequam,.

la:adj:ingratus.html:
in-grātus, a, um, adj.
Unpleasant, disagreeable (class. in prose and poetry).
Of things: bene quae in me fecerunt, ingrata habui,: sin autem ingrata esse sentiam,: fuit haec oratio non ingrata Gallis. : ingratam Veneri pone superbiam,: labor,: jocus,: sapor,.—
Of persons: non ingratus, acceptable, agreeable: Gaetulicus exercitui, (30). —
Unthankful, ungrateful.
Lit.: ingratus est, qui beneficium accepisse se negat, quod accepit: ingratus qui dissimulat: ingratus qui non reddit: ingratissimus omnium, qui oblitus est,: nihil cognovi ingratius,: ingrati animi crimen,: ingratum esse in aliquem,; ; : contra aliquem,: vir adversus merita Caesaris ingratissimus,; cf. , ext. 2: quia nihil amas, quom ingratum amas,irresponsive, who makes no return,.—
With gen.: salutis,not grateful for his preservation,. —
Pass., that receives no thanks: ingrata atque inrita esse omnia intellego quae dedi,: donum,: umeri,. —
Transf., of inanimate things that do not repay the trouble bestowed upon them, ungrateful: ager, that

bears nothing, : amicitiae,: ignosces tamen post, et id ingratum,you will get no thanks for it,: pericla,: cubile,: ingratā ingluvie rem stringere (i. e. quae numquam satiatur, numquam acceptis contenta est),insatiable,: ingrato vocem prostituisse foro,: mulier contra patronum suum ingrata,.— Hence, adv.: ingrātē.

Unpleasantly, disagreeably: ingrate viridis gemma,: sunt quibus ingrate timida indulgentia servit,: non ingrate nominando Varrone,not unwillingly, (al. in grege).—
Unthankfully, ungratefully: ingrate nostra facilitate abutuntur,: aliquid ferre,to receive a thing with unthankfulness,: ut sucus qui ingrate his (pomis vitiosis) posset impendi, ad meliora vertatur,.

la:verb:ingredior.gloss: to go into or onto, enter
senses: to go into or onto, enter
to enter upon, engage in, apply oneself to something
to go along, advance, proceed, march
to sleep with, go in unto
la:verb:ingredior.html:
in-grĕdĭor, essus 3, (in tmesi:
ut velit ire inque gredi,), v. dep. n. and a. [1. in-gradior]
Prop., to go into, to enter (class.; syn. intro, introeo).
With in and acc.: in stadium,: in templum,: in navem,: cum in antiquum fundum ingredi vellet, frequentes armati obstiterunt,; : in castra,: in urbem,.—
With acc.: iter pedibus,: domum,: pontem Mulvium,: via, quam nobis quoque ingrediendum sit,: hoc mare,: mare,: regnum,: curiam,; ; ; —
With intra: ingrediens intra finem ejus loci,: ingredi intra munitiones,: intra fines,.—
With dat.: castris ingressus Etruscis,. —
With ad: ad quos (sc. deos penates) paulo ante ingressus hospitaliter fecerat,.—
To enter upon, engage in, apply one's self to a thing.
With in and acc. (so most freq.): in vitam paulo serius, tanquam in viam, ingressus,: jam ingrediar in disputationem,: in eam rationem, : in spem libertatis,: in orationem,: in bellum,: in causam,; ; : in sermonem,: in rem publicam,to engage in public affairs,.—
With simple acc.: quam quisque viam vivendi sit ingressurus,: disputationem mecum,: vitam,; : magistratum,: consulatum,: eadem pericula,: hanc partem,: studia,: hunc video mihi principem ad ingrediendam rationem horum studiorum exstitisse,: eloquendi rationem,—
With ad: ad discendum,.—
To enter upon, begin, commence an action, speech, etc.
With inf.: posteaquam sum ingressus eas res mandare monumentis,: dicere,: describere aliquid,: scribere,; : versare dolos,.—
Absol.: sic contra est ingressa Venus, thus began Venus (to speak), : Anchises lacrimis ingressus obortis,.—
With acc.: quam orationem cum ingressus essem,: tibi res antiquae laudis et artis Ingredior,: longinquam profectionem,.—
With in and acc.: quem ingressum in sermonem Pompeius interpellavit,at the beginning of his speech,; cf. 1, 2, 2.—
Of time, to enter upon, begin, commence: Caesar decimum nonum annum ingressus,: ingresso vere, when spring has begun or arrived, .—
Transf., = incedo.— Prop., to go along, advance, proceed, march.
Absol.: si stas, ingredere; si ingrederis, curre,.—
With per: rex pedes per nivem et glaciem ingredi coepit,.—
With adv.: tardius,: quacumque,: elephanti gregatim ingrediuntur,.—
With abl.: campo,: solo,; 10, 767.—
Fig., to walk, go.
With abl.: vestigiis patris,; for which,
With acc.: vestigia patris,to follow, walk in,.—
With per: per titulos ingredimurque tuos,.—
Absol.: sublimia debent ingredi, lenia duci, acria currere, delicata fluere,to march majestically,: nec tragoedia socco ingreditur,.

la:noun:ingressus.html:
ingressus, ūs, m.
id.
,
a going into, entering, an entrance.
Lit.: Antonii in castra,: turba ad ingressum tuum te consalutavit,; fin.: haec in ipso ingressu meo (sc. in provinciam) scripsi,.— Esp.
A hostile entrance, inroad: ingressus hostiles,.—
A going, walking, gait: ingressus, cursus, accubitio, etc.,: prohiberi ingressu,were prevented from moving, could not stir a step,; cf.: instabilemque ingressum praebere,; so, praebere ingressum,: quaedam terrae ad ingressus tremunt,: celsior,. —
Transf., the way into a place, entrance, passage: trini ingressus,; cf.: vulgus quod Horatius arcet ingressu, ep. —
Trop., an entering upon any thing, beginning, commencement: in ingressu,: in ingressu (causae) ac fine,: in ingresssu operis,: ingressus capere,: Cannensis pugnae temerarius ingressus,.

la:verb:ingressus.html:
ingressus, ūs, m.
id.
,
a going into, entering, an entrance.
Lit.: Antonii in castra,: turba ad ingressum tuum te consalutavit,; fin.: haec in ipso ingressu meo (sc. in provinciam) scripsi,.— Esp.
A hostile entrance, inroad: ingressus hostiles,.—

la:verb:ingemo.gloss: to groan, moan or sigh (at or over)
senses: to groan, moan or sigh (at or over)
la:verb:ingemo.html:
in-gĕmo, ŭi, 3, v. a. and n.,
to groan or sigh over a thing; to mourn over, lament, bewail.
Act.: alicujus interitum,: caesos ingemunt nati patres,: jacentem,.— With inf.: ingemuit citro non satis esse suo,.—
Neutr., to mourn, groan, wail, lament: in aliqua re,: agris,.—With dat.: exsiliis alicujus,: ingemens laboribus,: conditioni suae,; : aratro,.—
Transf., of inanim. things: ingemuit solum,: limen,: omne nemus ingemuit alis,.

la:adj:ingens.html:
ingens, tis, adj.
2. in-genus, gens, that goes beyond its kind or species, qs. uncouth, monstrous
,
of immoderate size, vast, huge, prodigious, enormous; great, remarkable: magnas vero agere gratias Thais mihi? Gn. Ingentes, (cf.: satis erat respondere magnas: ingentes inquit, semper auget assentator,): ingens immanisque praeda,: ingens immensusque campus,: pecunia,an exorbitant sum,; cf. : aquae,: aequor,: pinus,: exitus Istri,: clamor,: gloria,: virtus atque animus,: ingentia facta,: vir,: ingens aliquā re, great, remarkable, distinguished in any respect: vir famā ingens, ingentior armis,: gloriā,: viribus opibusque,: eloquio,.—
With gen.: ingens virium atque animi, Dietsch: femina

ingens animi, : vir ingens rerum,.—

With inf.: ingens ferre mala,.—Comp. (poet.), .—
Trop., great, strong, powerful: senatus,: Paulus,: ingentis spiritus vir,: cui genus a proavis ingens,.

la:verb:ingemino.html:
in-gĕmĭno, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. and n.,
to redouble, repeat, reiterate.
Act.: dextrā ingeminans ictus,: terrorem,: liquidas voces,: vox assensu nemorum ingeminata remugit,: me miserum! ingeminat,; . —
Neutr., to be redoubled, to increase: ingeminant austri,: ingeminant plausu Tyrii,: ignes,: clamor,: ingeminant curae,.
la:verb:ingemino.inflection: āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. and n.

la:verb:ingruo.html:
ingrŭo, ŭi, 3, v. n.
in-ruo, with an epenth. g from gruo, kindr. with κρούω
,
to rush or break into, to fall violently upon, assail, attack (syn. incumbo; differing from immineo and impendo, in that it denotes the actual doing of that which they merely threaten; not in Cic. or Cæs.).
Lit.: hostes crebri cadunt; nostri contra ingruunt,: ingruit Aeneas Italis,; cf.: ingruere hostes,: simul ingruunt saxa jaciunt,: ingruentes accusatores,: ingruente in Italiam Hannibale,.—
Transf., of things: ferreus ingruit imber,: umbra vitibus,: nox,: tela,: ingruere morbi in remiges coeperunt,: si bellum ingrueret,; : si nullus ingruat metus,: si quid subitum ingruat,: damnatio,.

la:verb:ingemesco.gloss: to (begin to) groan or moan at or over

la:verb:ingemisco.gloss: to (begin to) groan or moan at or over
senses: to (begin to) groan or moan at or over
la:verb:ingemisco.html:
in-gĕmisco, ŭi, 3. v. a. and n.,
to groan or sigh over a thing.
Act.
With acc. and inf.: quid ingemiscis hostem Dolabellam judicatum,: ingemuit citro non satis esse suo,. —
With acc. obj.: suos casus,.—Hence, ingĕmiscendus, a, um, lamentable: clades,.—
Neutr.: pueri Spartani non ingemiscunt,: quantum ingemiscant patres nostri, si, etc.,: in quo tu ingemiscis,.—With dat.: ulli malo, (a transl. from Sophocles): ingemiscamus illis, quae patiebamur,.—With ad: ad aliquid,ext.—With abl.: (luce) repertā,: morte alicujus,. —
Transf., of inanim. things: ignis ingemiscit,.

la:verb:ingredere.gloss: second-person singular present active imperative/indicative of ingredior
senses: second-person singular present active imperative/indicative of ingredior

la:adj:inglorius.html:
inglōrĭus, a, um, adj.
2. in-gloria
,
without glory or fame, not glorious, inglorious.
Lit. (class.): beati qui honorati sunt videntur; miseri qui sunt inglorii,: latam trahens inglorius alvum,: imperium, Tac A. 12, 14: vita inhouorata et ingloria,. —
With gen.: militiae,: ausi,.—
Transf.: ingloria cassis,unadorned, without a crest,.

la:verb:ingero.gloss: to carry, pour or throw in or into
senses: to carry, pour or throw in or into
la:verb:ingero.html:
in-gĕro, gessi, gestum, 3, v. a. (
imper. inger for ingere, ), to carry, pour, throw, or put into, in, or upon a place.
Lit.
In gen.: aquam ingere,: ligna foco,: quicquid vini oleique erat, oribus ingerebatur,: e puteis aquam in salinas,.—
Esp.
Ingerere se, to betake one's self or rush to any place: ubi confertissimos hostes pugnare conspexisset, eo se semper ingerebat,: se morti obviam,; cf.: se oculis, to offer one's self to, : sese periclis,.—
To inflict upon, execute, apply: supplicia,: pugnos alicui in ventrem,to deal blows,: verbera, Curt. 6, 11, 8: manus capiti,—
Of weapons, to press upon, thrust into: ensem viris,: hastas in tergum fugientibus,: saxa in subeuntes,: sagittas et jacula,: missilia in propugnantes,; .—
To bring, give, or present to one: saginandis anseribus polentae duas partes, et furfuris quatuor ingerunt,: mihi nova pocula,.—Absol.: aqua frigida ingesta sistitur sanguis,administered internally,.—
To bring, throw, heap, or put upon a person or thing: ut Cassandreus, saucius ingestā contumuleris humo,: vasta giganteis ingesta est insula membris,: adeps pastillis ingestus,: stercus vitibus,: summis ingestum montibus Aepy,: facies ingesta sopori,: ingesta vincula unguibus,: supplicia,. —
Trop.
In gen., of language.
To pour forth, to pour out against: convicia alicui,: contumelias,: vocis verborumque quantum voletis,. —
To mention, repeat, keep saying: auctorem suum ingerit et inculcat,: ingerebat lentissima voce, Carpe, Carpe,; : omnia mala ingerebat,: voces quae plerumque verae et graves coram ingerebantur,: a tribunis eadem ingerebantur,.—
In partic.
To obtrude, press, or force upon one: ne recusanti quidem amicitiam suam ingerere destitit, Roth: nomina liberis,; cf. : filium filiamque orbis senibus,: omnia imperia recusanti,: ingerebat iste Artemidorum,: his se ingerit (Fortuna),presses her favors,: veritatis tanta vis est ut nemo ... qui non videat ingerentem se oculis divinam claritatem,: nomen patris patriae a populo saepius ingestum repudiavit,pressed upon him,.—
To heap up: scelus sceleri,.

la:noun:inguen.html:
inguen, inis, n. (also late Lat. inguĭ-na, ae, f., ),
the front part of the body between the hips.
Lit.
The groin.— Sing., : lentum destillat ab inguine virus,; more freq. plur.: candida succincta inguina (Scylla),: ventrem atque inguina hausit,; —
The privy members, ; ; ; —
A swelling in the groin, Lucil. ap. Müll.; ; also a swelling on the knee, , ep. 44 Mai.—
The abdomen: legenti suffodit inguina,; . —
Transf., of plants, the place where a branch is joined to the stem, ; .

la:verb:ingravo.html:
in-grăvo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. (poet. and in post-Aug. prose).
To weigh down: puppem,.—
Transf.
To cause its weight to be felt, to oppress, molest: saevitia hiemis ingravat,: annis ingravantibus,.—
To render worse, to aggravate: ingravat haec saevus Drances,: illa meos casus ingravat, illa levat,.—
To make severe (eccl. Lat.): ingravavit cor suum,he hardened his heart,; in pass.,

la:verb:ingravesco.html:
in-grăvesco, 3 (in tmesi:
inque gravescunt,), v. inch. n., to grow heavy, become heavier.
Lit.: corpora exercitationum defatigatione ingravescunt,: sal vix incredibili pondere ingravescit,. — Poet., to become pregnant: suscipiunt aliae pondus magis inque gravescunt,.—
Transf., to increase; grow worse, to become burdensome: ingravescens morbus,: ingravescens aetas,: corpora exercitationum defetigatione ingravescunt,: hoc studium quotidie ingravescit,grows more serious,: alter in dies ingravescit,: annona, provisions grow dearer, Auct. Or. pro Domo, 5, 11: Verania mox ingravescit, clamat moriens, etc.,: falsis (rumoribus) ingravescebat,by false reports he sank deeper and deeper,.

la:adj:ingeniosior.gloss: superior in intellect, gifted with genius; intellectual, clever, ingenious

senses: to plunge oneself into something, to addict oneself
la:verb:ingurgito.html:
ingurgĭto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.
in-gurges
,
to pour in like a flood or whirlpool.
Lit.: merum ventri suo,: vide ut avariter merum in se ingurgitat faucibus plenis,: umor ex nivibus non universus ingurgitans (sc. se), diluensque, sed destillans,.—
To flood, to fill: Rhodanus palude sese ingurgitat, nomine Lemanno,.—
To glut or gorge one's self with meat and drink, to gormandize, guzzle: se caeno (of swine),: crudique postridie se rursus ingurgitant,: ingenium crebris et ingentibus poculis,.— Hence, ingurgitari, to make one's self drunk, to get drunk: anus ingurgitata,: temeto ingurgitatus,.—
Trop., to engage deeply in, be absorbed in any thing, to addict or devote one's self to: se in flagitia,: se in alicujus copias,: qui degustandum ex philosophia censet, non in eam ingurgitandum, (cf. Rib. ad loc.).

la:adj:ingeniosissimus.gloss: superior in intellect, gifted with genius; intellectual, clever, ingenious

la:verb:ingigno.html:
in-gigno, gĕnŭi, gĕnĭtum, 3, v. a.,
to instil by birth or nature, to implant, engender.
Lit.: herbasque nocentes rupibus ingenuit tellus,: vites ingenita sterilitate,.—
Trop.: natura cupiditatem nomini ingenuit,: tantam ingenuit animantibus conservandi sui natura custodiam,: vitia ingenita,inborn,: cum sic hominis natura generata sit, ut habeat quiddam ingenitum quasi civile atque populare,innate,.

la:verb:ingenero.html:
in-gĕnĕro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.
To implant, engender, produce.
Lit.: natura ingenerat amorem in eos qui, etc.,: homini soli cupiditas ingeneratur, id. Fragm. ap. : non ingenerantur hominibus mores,: ingenerata familiae frugalitas,: haec astro ingenerata,.—
Transf., to generate, create: animum esse ingeneratum a Deo,: societas quam ingeneravit natura,.—
Transf., to plant.— Absol.: ingenera; nunc sunt genitalia tempora mundi (sc. tellurem),.

la:noun:ingenuitas.gloss: The condition of being free-born or noble
senses: The condition of being free-born or noble
la:noun:ingenuitas.html:
ingĕnŭĭtas, ātis, f.
id.
.
The condition of a free-born man or gentleman, good birth: ornamenta ingenuitatis,: assertus in ingenuitatem,; .—
Trop., a mode of thinking worthy of a freeman, noble-mindedness,frankness, ingenuousness, noble demeanor: prae se probitatem quandam et ingenuitatem ferre,; : praestare ingenuitatem et ruborem,.

la:noun:ingratia.html:
ingrātĭa, ae, f.
ingratus
.
Thanklessness, ingratitude: in ingratiam incidere,: hominum,.—Hence,
ingrātĭīs, or contr. ingrātīs (v. Zumpt ad ), without one's thanks, against one's will.
As subst. (rare, and not in class. Lat.): tuis ingratiis ( = te invito),; so perh. ingratiis nostris,.— With gen.: vobis invitis atque amborum ingratiis,.—
Adv., unwillingly, against his (her, etc.) will (class., and in both forms): id quod odio'st faciundum'st cum malo atque ingratiis,; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; : ingratis,; ; : extorquendum est invito atque ingratiis,: dicent quae necesse erit, ingratiis, Halm (Zumpt, ingratis): nisi plane cogit ingratiis, id. Tull. § 5; cf.: ut ingratis ad depugnandum omnes cogerentur,against their will,; so, cogere, also . —See Hand, Turs. III. p. 379 sq.
